titleStmt.title: A synaptic and circuit basis for corollary discharge in the auditory cortex
titleStmt.author: Schneider
Nelson
Mooney

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: A synaptic and circuit basis for corollary discharge in the auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how a copy of the motor command reaches auditory cortex and what it does to hearing during movement
span.quote: In mammals, signals propagating from the motor cortex to the auditory cortex are thought to play a critical role in normal hearing and behavior, yet the synaptic and circuit mechanisms by which these motor-related signals influence auditory cortical activity remain poorly understood.

span.label: which synapses and which circuit carry the motor-related suppression of auditory cortical responses
span.quote: Despite the widespread observation that movement can modulate auditory cortical activity and the presumed role of the motor cortex in driving this modulation, the synaptic and circuit mechanisms by which the motor cortex influences auditory cortical activity during movement remain unresolved.

span.label: identifies the suppression as postsynaptic inhibition from local PV interneurons, driven by a specific set of secondary motor cortex neurons that project to auditory cortex and fire before movement
span.quote: Electrophysiology and optogenetic gain- and loss-of-function experiments reveal that motor-related changes in auditory cortical dynamics are driven by a subset of neurons in the secondary motor cortex that innervate the auditory cortex and are active during movement.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Using in vivo intracellular recordings in behaving mice, we find that excitatory neurons in the auditory cortex are suppressed prior to and during movement, due in part to increased activity of local parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons.

span.label: motor-related corollary discharge in auditory cortex
span.quote: We found that a wide variety of natural movements strongly suppresses the spontaneous and tone-evoked synaptic activity of auditory cortical excitatory cells and that a substantial fraction of this suppression is mediated through a postsynaptic mechanism involving increased local inhibition via PV+ interneurons.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Here we combine in vivo intracellular physiology with optogenetic circuit manipulations in freely behaving mice to identify a synaptic signature of movement in the auditory cortex and to elucidate local and long-range circuits that modulate auditory cortical activity during movement.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Motor-related signals from secondary motor cortex excite PV+ interneurons in auditory cortex, which postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells and thereby suppress both spontaneous and sound-evoked activity
span.quote: These experiments indicate that in the auditory cortex, motor-related signals excite PV+ interneurons, which in turn postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells to suppress their spontaneous activity and stimulus-evoked responses.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Transient motor-driven dampening of sensitivity to self-predictable quiet sounds preserves headroom for responding to unexpected loud stimuli
span.quote: may reflect a general strategy where motor-related signals transiently dampen sensitivity to predictable low-intensity sounds, enabling auditory neurons to maintain responsiveness to unexpected high-intensity stimuli

span.label: motor-related signals excite PV interneurons, which postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells and suppress both spontaneous and evoked activity
span.quote: These experiments indicate that in the auditory cortex, motor-related signals excite PV+ interneurons, which in turn postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells to suppress their spontaneous activity and stimulus-evoked responses.

span.label: the inhibitory cells fire well before movement onset and before the excitatory cells fall below baseline, in the order M2 then PV then excitatory
span.quote: As a population, inhibitory neuron firing rates increased well before movement onset and also before the firing rates of auditory cortical excitatory cells decreased below their baseline levels (−805 ms for PV+ cells, −605 ms for VGAT+ cells, and −490 ms for excitatory cells, relative to movement onset).

span.label: the movement-related voltage change reverses near the chloride equilibrium potential, which is what identifies the inhibition as postsynaptic
span.quote: The movement-related change in mean membrane potential reversed in sign at ~ −72 mV, which was 3 mV depolarized relative to the average resting Vm and close to the chloride equilibrium potential reported for mouse auditory cortical pyramidal neurons

span.label: the suppression may dampen sensitivity to predictable quiet sounds while preserving responsiveness to unexpected loud ones
span.quote: Notably, whereas the gain of stimulus-evoked responses in visual cortical pyramidal cells increases with locomotion 5 , 25 , perhaps to compensate for increased visual flow, auditory cortical responses to tones decreased during movement. This suppressive effect, which resembles corollary discharge signals described in the auditory systems of animals ranging from insects to humans 6 , 41 , may reflect a general strategy where motor-related signals transiently dampen sensitivity to predictable low-intensity sounds, enabling auditory neurons to maintain responsiveness to unexpected high-intensity stimuli

span.label: the mechanism differs from the disinhibition proposed for locomotion-driven gain increases in visual cortex
span.quote: This mechanism contrasts with a disinhibitory mechanism implicated in locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses 38 , with a parallel negative rescaling of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive that has been advanced to account for state-dependent changes in auditory cortical responsiveness 23 , and with presynaptic depression driven by state-dependent increases in thalamic activity

span.label: The evidence establishes postsynaptic inhibition but does not exclude a presynaptic contribution.
span.note: what this limits: the mechanism of the suppression: the features INDICATE ... POSTSYNAPTIC INHIBITION, BUT DO NOT EXCLUDE THE POSSIBILITY THAT PRESYNAPTIC INHIBITION IS ALSO INVOLVED
span.quote: All of these features indicate that motor-related signals suppress auditory cortical excitatory cells via postsynaptic inhibition, but do not exclude the possibility that presynaptic inhibition is also involved.

span.label: Animals were not randomised to groups and investigators were not blinded to group allocation.
span.note: what this limits: every group comparison in the paper: RANDOMIZATION WAS NOT USED TO DETERMINE HOW ANIMALS WERE ALLOCATED TO EXPERIMENTAL GROUPS, NOR WERE INVESTIGATORS BLINDED TO GROUP ALLOCATION
span.quote: Randomization was not used to determine how animals were allocated to experimental groups, nor were investigators blinded to group allocation.

span.label: Optogenetic terminal stimulation could in principle recruit indirect pathways via antidromic activation (argued against by two control observations).
span.note: what this limits: the terminal-stimulation results: OPTOGENETIC ACTIVATION OF M2 TERMINALS ... TRIGGERS ANTIDROMIC PROPAGATION ... AND THUS EXCITES OTHER TARGETS OF M2 ACtx CELLS
span.quote: One potential concern is that optogenetic activation of M2 terminals in the auditory cortex triggers antidromic propagation of action potentials and thus excites other targets of M2 ACtx cells, some of which may also innervate the auditory cortex.

span.label: postsynaptic inhibition is established but presynaptic inhibition is not excluded outright
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - postsynaptic inhibition is established, presynaptic is not excluded
span.quote: All of these features indicate that motor-related signals suppress auditory cortical excitatory cells via postsynaptic inhibition, but do not exclude the possibility that presynaptic inhibition is also involved.

span.label: M2 could also act indirectly through neuromodulatory cell groups, which the design does not rule out
span.note: what this limits: the direct-pathway interpretation: M2 COULD ALSO ACT INDIRECTLY THROUGH OR IN CONCERT WITH NEUROMODULATORY CELL GROUPS
span.quote: However, M2 and the auditory cortex are embedded in complex networks, a consequence of which is that in addition to directly influencing auditory cortical processing, M2 could also act indirectly through or in concert with neuromodulatory cell groups 40 to modulate auditory cortical dynamics.

span.label: vocalizations were always accompanied by other movements, so no vocalization-specific signal could be isolated
span.note: what this limits: any vocalisation-specific reading: VOCALIZATIONS WERE ALWAYS ACCOMPANIED BY OTHER HEAD AND BODY MOVEMENTS, and the membrane potential dynamics WERE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THOSE OBSERVED DURING HEAD MOVEMENTS
span.quote: We also were able to elicit vocalizations in a subset of experiments (5 neurons in 3 mice) and although vocalizations were always accompanied by other head and body movements, the membrane potential dynamics during vocalization were indistinguishable from those observed during head movements, body movements, and translocation

span.label: excitatory cells were identified by intrinsic and firing properties, with staining in only a subset
span.note: what this limits: results reported by cell class: cells were CLASSIFIED AS PUTATIVE EXCITATORY CELLS BASED ON THEIR INTRINSIC PROPERTIES ... AND, IN A SUBSET OF NEURONS, INTRACELLULAR STAINING
span.quote: cells were classified as putative excitatory cells based on their intrinsic properties, spontaneous and DC-evoked action potential patterns and, in a subset of neurons, intracellular staining and post-hoc visualization

span.label: corollary discharge as a framework, imported from systems where the motor copy is a single identified neuron
span.quote: Notably, whereas the gain of stimulus-evoked responses in visual cortical pyramidal cells increases with locomotion 5 , 25 , perhaps to compensate for increased visual flow, auditory cortical responses to tones decreased during movement. This suppressive effect, which resembles corollary discharge signals described in the auditory systems of animals ranging from insects to humans 6 , 41 , may reflect a general strategy where motor-related signals transiently dampen sensitivity to predictable low-intensity sounds, enabling auditory neurons to maintain responsiveness to unexpected high-intensity stimuli

span.label: terminal stimulation used to bypass a pathway rather than to activate a region, isolating where an effect arises
span.quote: Whereas acoustic stimulation activates the auditory system from the periphery to the cortex, this optogenetic approach allowed us to effectively bypass the ascending auditory pathway prior to the thalamocortical projection and to thus isolate the component of motor-related suppression that occurs within the auditory cortex.

span.label: corollary discharge here means a motor-related signal that PRECEDES movement, which is what distinguishes it from sensory reafference caused by the movement
span.quote: The finding that changes in auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics preceded locomotion onset by several to many hundreds of milliseconds indicates they cannot be caused by sensory reafference generated by the ensuing movements, and instead could reflect a motor-related signal.

span.label: the local share of the suppression is quantified rather than asserted: about 60 percent arises inside auditory cortex, the rest elsewhere in the pathway
span.quote: We also found that the degree of suppression of optogenetically evoked activity during movement was linearly related to the degree of suppression of tone-evoked activity during movement (slope = 0.6), indicating that approximately 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses in auditory cortical excitatory neurons arises through mechanisms local to the auditory cortex

span.label: M2 ACtx cells are a subset defined by their projection target, identified by an intersectional strategy, and behave like the general M2 population
span.quote: Two-photon calcium imaging of GCaMP6s-expressing M2 neurons in head-fixed mice running on a treadmill revealed that M2 ACtx cells exhibited movement-related increases in fluorescence with a time course indistinguishable from that of the general M2 population

span.label: movement here spans locomotion, head and body movements, grooming and vocalization, all producing indistinguishable auditory cortical dynamics
span.quote: We also were able to elicit vocalizations in a subset of experiments (5 neurons in 3 mice) and although vocalizations were always accompanied by other head and body movements, the membrane potential dynamics during vocalization were indistinguishable from those observed during head movements, body movements, and translocation

span.label: the head-fixed treadmill preparation was validated against the freely behaving one before being used for the optogenetics
span.quote: The changes in membrane potential dynamics in the auditory cortex of head-fixed mice during treadmill locomotion, grooming, facial movements, posturing and forelimb movements were indistinguishable from those we observed in unrestrained, freely behaving mice, were consistent across superficial and deeper cortical layers

span.label: claim_type: mechanism
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: mechanism — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: By applying a wide range of electrophysiological, optical, optogenetic and pharmacological methods in the freely behaving mouse, this study identifies a postsynaptic inhibitory signature of motor action within auditory cortex, a local source of this inhibition, and a long-range motor-to-auditory cortical circuit that engages this local inhibitory mechanism to suppress tone-evoked responses during movement.

span.label: method: sharp-electrode intracellular recording in freely behaving and head-fixed mice, with optogenetic activation and silencing, multielectrode arrays and two-photon imaging
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: electrophysiology — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: By applying a wide range of electrophysiological, optical, optogenetic and pharmacological methods in the freely behaving mouse, this study identifies a postsynaptic inhibitory signature of motor action within auditory cortex, a local source of this inhibition, and a long-range motor-to-auditory cortical circuit that engages this local inhibitory mechanism to suppress tone-evoked responses during movement.

span.label: phenomenon: suppression of auditory cortical responses before and during movement
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: motor-related corollary discharge in auditory cortex — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Using in vivo intracellular recordings in behaving mice, we find that excitatory neurons in the auditory cortex are suppressed prior to and during movement, due in part to increased activity of local parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons.

span.label: contradicts → the disinhibitory mechanism proposed for locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses (ref. 38), the negative-rescaling account of state-dependent auditory cortical changes (ref. 23) and presynaptic depression from state-dependent thalamic activity (ref. 30)
span.quote: This mechanism contrasts with a disinhibitory mechanism implicated in locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses 38 , with a parallel negative rescaling of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive that has been advanced to account for state-dependent changes in auditory cortical responsiveness 23 , and with presynaptic depression driven by state-dependent increases in thalamic activity 30 .

span.label: builds-on → the prior anatomical finding that the M2-to-auditory-cortex projection is almost completely ipsilateral (ref. 20)
span.quote: These differential effects of silencing ipsilateral versus contralateral M2 on auditory cortical dynamics are consistent with a previous anatomical finding that the projection from M2 to auditory cortex is almost completely ipsilateral 20 .

span.label: extends → observations of movement-related modulation of auditory cortex in monkeys and humans (refs. 1, 10, 11, 18, 37), for which a direct motor-cortical role had not been tested
span.quote: Although movement-related modulation of auditory cortical activity has been detected in monkey and human auditory cortex during a variety of behaviors 1 , 10 , 11 , 18 , 37 , a direct role for the motor cortex in these modulatory processes was untested.

span.label: contradicts → sensory reafference and peripheral masking as explanations for movement-related auditory suppression
span.quote: The finding that changes in auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics preceded locomotion onset by several to many hundreds of milliseconds indicates they cannot be caused by sensory reafference generated by the ensuing movements, and instead could reflect a motor-related signal.

span.label: distinguishes-from → the disinhibitory account of locomotion-driven gain increases in visual cortex
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE CIRCUIT MECHANISM, WITH BOTH NAMED. 'THIS MECHANISM CONTRASTS WITH A DISINHIBITORY MECHANISM implicated in locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses, WITH A PARALLEL NEGATIVE RESCALING OF EXCITATORY AND INHIBITORY SYNAPTIC DRIVE that has been advanced to account for STATE-DEPENDENT CHANGES.' Two accounts of behaviour-driven cortical change that predict opposite things about inhibition - so a result reported as `state-dependent modulation` is compatible with either until the inhibitory drive is measured. Q-500.
span.quote: This mechanism contrasts with a disinhibitory mechanism implicated in locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses 38 , with a parallel negative rescaling of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive that has been advanced to account for state-dependent changes in auditory cortical responsiveness 23 , and with presynaptic depression driven by state-dependent increases in thalamic activity

span.label: extends → anesthetized-mouse work showing motor cortical synapses suppress tone-evoked auditory responses
span.quote: In mammals, signals propagating from the motor cortex to the auditory cortex are thought to play a critical role in normal hearing and behavior, yet the synaptic and circuit mechanisms by which these motor-related signals influence auditory cortical activity remain poorly understood.

span.label: supports → corollary discharge accounts described across species from insects to humans
span.quote: Notably, whereas the gain of stimulus-evoked responses in visual cortical pyramidal cells increases with locomotion 5 , 25 , perhaps to compensate for increased visual flow, auditory cortical responses to tones decreased during movement. This suppressive effect, which resembles corollary discharge signals described in the auditory systems of animals ranging from insects to humans 6 , 41 , may reflect a general strategy where motor-related signals transiently dampen sensitivity to predictable low-intensity sounds, enabling auditory neurons to maintain responsiveness to unexpected high-intensity stimuli

span.label: builds-on → anatomical tracing showing the M2-to-auditory projection is almost entirely ipsilateral
span.quote: These differential effects of silencing ipsilateral versus contralateral M2 on auditory cortical dynamics are consistent with a previous anatomical finding that the projection from M2 to auditory cortex is almost completely ipsilateral

span.label: corollary discharge —distinct-from→ reafference
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: temporal precedence. The signal leads movement by over 200 ms, so it cannot be caused by the movement's own sound
span.quote: The finding that changes in auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics preceded locomotion onset by several to many hundreds of milliseconds indicates they cannot be caused by sensory reafference generated by the ensuing movements, and instead could reflect a motor-related signal.

span.label: masking —distinct-from→ reafference
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — a second, independent exclusion: the effect survives noise loud enough to mask tone responses
span.quote: Moreover, movement-related changes in auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics persisted in the presence of broadband noise that was sufficiently loud to mask tone-evoked responses, further supporting the motor-related nature of these signals

span.label: M2 —causes→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: These experiments indicate that in the auditory cortex, motor-related signals excite PV+ interneurons, which in turn postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells to suppress their spontaneous activity and stimulus-evoked responses.

span.label: PV+ —causes→ excitatory neurons
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — SIGN: suppressive, and the firing order M2 then PV then excitatory matches the proposed direction
span.quote: Before and during movements, the firing rates of PV+ cells and other fast-spiking interneurons increased, whereas the firing rates of putative excitatory neurons decreased

span.label: membrane potential —operationalised-as→ PV+
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — the reversal near the chloride equilibrium potential is what makes the inhibition postsynaptic rather than inferred
span.quote: The movement-related change in mean membrane potential reversed in sign at ~ −72 mV, which was 3 mV depolarized relative to the average resting Vm and close to the chloride equilibrium potential reported for mouse auditory cortical pyramidal neurons

span.label: thalamocortical —part-of→ auditory cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — stimulating these terminals bypasses everything below them, which is how the local share of the suppression is isolated
span.quote: Whereas acoustic stimulation activates the auditory system from the periphery to the cortex, this optogenetic approach allowed us to effectively bypass the ascending auditory pathway prior to the thalamocortical projection and to thus isolate the component of motor-related suppression that occurs within the auditory cortex.

span.label: presynaptic depression —operationalised-as→ onset slope
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION, and the assay was VALIDATED FIRST: 20 Hz stimulation was shown to change the slope before the absence of a change was claimed as a null
span.quote: To explore this possibility we first established that optogenetically stimulating auditory thalamocortical synapses at > 20 Hz was sufficient to decrease the onset slope of the evoked EPSP, which provides a postsynaptic readout of presynaptic depression

span.label: TTX —distinct-from→ antidromic
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — silencing the cell bodies leaves the terminal effect intact, so the effect is not routed through M2 somata
span.quote: First, optogenetic activation of M2 terminals was equally efficacious in modulating auditory cortical dynamics when M2 cell bodies were pharmacologically silenced with the sodium channel blocker TTX

span.label: antidromic —distinct-from→ auditory cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: the effect appears in under 7 ms and antidromic propagation takes about 12, so it is too fast to be indirect
span.quote: Second, the onset of changes in auditory cortical dynamics following optogenetic activation of M2 terminals occurred more rapidly (<7 ms) than the antidromic propagation time from auditory cortex to M2 (~12 ms)

span.label: visual cortex —contrasted-with→ auditory cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — SIGN REVERSAL: the same manipulation raises gain in one sensory cortex and lowers it in the other
span.quote: In contrast to findings in the visual cortex, stimulus (i.e., tone)-evoked synaptic responses of auditory cortical excitatory neurons were significantly diminished during movements

span.label: M2 —causes→ locomotion
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — silencing either side stops movement within about 500 ms, which is why the ipsilateral-only auditory effect is informative
span.quote: To test this idea, we unilaterally and selectively silenced M2 excitatory neuron cell bodies during locomotion by optogenetically activating M2 inhibitory neurons in VGAT-ChR2 mice ( Fig. 5a–c , Extended Data Fig. 8e ). Silencing either ipsilateral or contralateral M2 (relative to the auditory cortical recording site) was sufficient to arrest movements ~500 ms after light onset

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Student’s t-test, paired t-test and Two-sampled t-test were used as described below.

span.label: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
span.quote: All distributions passed tests for normality (Kolmogorov-Smirnov).

span.label: significance level (alpha)
span.quote: For all statistical tests, significance was measured against alpha of 0.05.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: We ran a two-factor ANOVA with repeated measures to determine whether there was a significant interaction between laser stimulation and movement on auditory cortical dynamics when optogenetically silencing M2 in VGAT-ChR2 mice.

span.label: interaction effect
span.quote: Both analyses revealed significant interaction terms (p<0.05).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Statistical details for experiments described in Figures 1 – 5 are detailed below, including the sample size (number of neurons and number of mice), population mean +/− s.d. values, exact p-values and statistical tests.

span.label: percentile threshold
span.quote: Significance thresholds were determined by calculating the 95 th percentile of baseline firing rates for each population independently.

span.label: linear regression / slope
span.quote: We also found that the degree of suppression of optogenetically evoked activity during movement was linearly related to the degree of suppression of tone-evoked activity during movement (slope = 0.6), indicating that approximately 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses in auditory cortical excitatory neurons arises through mechanisms local to the auditory cortex

span.label: linearly related
span.quote: We also found that the degree of suppression of optogenetically evoked activity during movement was linearly related to the degree of suppression of tone-evoked activity during movement (slope = 0.6), indicating that approximately 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses in auditory cortical excitatory neurons arises through mechanisms local to the auditory cortex

span.label: Just before and during locomotion, head movements, grooming and other movements, auditory cortical excitatory neurons showed less variable membrane potentials and a slight depolarization.
span.quote: Immediately prior to and during a variety of movements including locomotion, head movements, and other body movements such as grooming, auditory excitatory neurons exhibited decreased variability in their subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations and a slight depolarization

span.label: These membrane potential changes began on average more than 200 ms before locomotion started and persisted about as long after it ended.
span.quote: By monitoring the onset and duration of locomotor bouts, we found that changes in membrane potential dynamics of auditory cortical excitatory neurons preceded locomotion on average by >200 ms and typically outlasted locomotion by a similar duration

span.label: Because the cortical changes precede movement onset by hundreds of milliseconds, they cannot be caused by sound or other sensory feedback from the movement itself and must instead be motor-related.
span.quote: The finding that changes in auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics preceded locomotion onset by several to many hundreds of milliseconds indicates they cannot be caused by sensory reafference generated by the ensuing movements, and instead could reflect a motor-related signal.

span.label: Unlike visual cortex, where locomotion boosts responses, tone-evoked synaptic responses of auditory cortical excitatory neurons were significantly reduced during movement.
span.quote: In contrast to findings in the visual cortex, stimulus (i.e., tone)-evoked synaptic responses of auditory cortical excitatory neurons were significantly diminished during movements

span.label: Roughly 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses originates within the auditory cortex itself rather than upstream, since optogenetically evoked thalamocortical responses were suppressed in proportion to tone responses.
span.quote: We also found that the degree of suppression of optogenetically evoked activity during movement was linearly related to the degree of suppression of tone-evoked activity during movement (slope = 0.6), indicating that approximately 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses in auditory cortical excitatory neurons arises through mechanisms local to the auditory cortex

span.label: The rising slope of thalamocortical EPSPs was unchanged between movement and rest, ruling out presynaptic depression of thalamic terminals as the cause of suppression.
span.quote: We then measured the onset slope of optogenetically-evoked thalamocortical synaptic potentials, and found no difference in the rising slope of the EPSP across movement and rest conditions, indicating that thalamic terminals in the auditory cortex are not depressed during movement

span.label: The movement-related membrane potential change reversed near -72 mV, close to the reported chloride equilibrium potential, pointing to a postsynaptic inhibitory (chloride-mediated) current.
span.quote: The movement-related change in mean membrane potential reversed in sign at ~ −72 mV, which was 3 mV depolarized relative to the average resting Vm and close to the chloride equilibrium potential reported for mouse auditory cortical pyramidal neurons

span.label: Around movement, PV+ and other fast-spiking interneurons in auditory cortex increased their firing while putative excitatory neurons decreased theirs.
span.quote: Before and during movements, the firing rates of PV+ cells and other fast-spiking interneurons increased, whereas the firing rates of putative excitatory neurons decreased

span.label: The inhibitory neurons' firing rose several hundred milliseconds before movement onset and before excitatory cells dropped below baseline, consistent with inhibition leading the suppression.
span.quote: As a population, inhibitory neuron firing rates increased well before movement onset and also before the firing rates of auditory cortical excitatory cells decreased below their baseline levels (−805 ms for PV+ cells, −605 ms for VGAT+ cells, and −490 ms for excitatory cells, relative to movement onset).

span.label: Excitatory neurons in secondary motor cortex increased their firing about 870 ms before movement onset, earlier than any of the auditory cortical changes.
span.quote: we determined that M2 excitatory neuron action potential activity increased prior to a variety of movements, including locomotion ( Fig. 3c ; −870 ms, relative to movement onset)

span.label: Optogenetically activating M2 axon terminals in the auditory cortex of a resting mouse reproduced the movement signature: reduced membrane potential variability, reduced tone-evoked responses and slight depolarization.
span.quote: optically activating ChR2+ M2 terminals in the auditory cortex of resting mice decreased the membrane potential variability and tone-evoked responses of excitatory cells and also resulted in a slight depolarization, highly similar to the effects of movement

span.label: The terminal-activation effect was not an indirect antidromic one: it survived pharmacological silencing of M2 cell bodies with TTX.
span.quote: First, optogenetic activation of M2 terminals was equally efficacious in modulating auditory cortical dynamics when M2 cell bodies were pharmacologically silenced with the sodium channel blocker TTX

span.label: The auditory cortical change began within 7 ms of terminal stimulation, faster than the roughly 12 ms antidromic conduction time back to M2, again excluding an indirect route.
span.quote: Second, the onset of changes in auditory cortical dynamics following optogenetic activation of M2 terminals occurred more rapidly (<7 ms) than the antidromic propagation time from auditory cortex to M2 (~12 ms)

span.label: Silencing ipsilateral M2 restored rest-like membrane potential dynamics in auditory cortex within about 70 ms of laser onset, before the animal actually stopped moving.
span.quote: Notably, silencing ipsilateral M2 rapidly (~70 ms after laser onset) restored rest-like membrane potential dynamics in the auditory cortex

span.label: Silencing ipsilateral M2 while the mouse was still moving recovered about 40 percent of the tone-evoked response, showing M2 activity is necessary for the movement-related gain reduction.
span.quote: Presenting tones during the initial phase of M2 suppression, when auditory cortical membrane potential dynamics had transitioned to a rest-like state but before locomotion offset, revealed a strong (~40 percent) recovery of tone-evoked responses

span.label: auditory cortical excitatory neurons are suppressed before and during movement, due in part to increased activity of local PV+ interneurons
span.quote: Using in vivo intracellular recordings in behaving mice, we find that excitatory neurons in the auditory cortex are suppressed prior to and during movement, due in part to increased activity of local parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons.

span.label: the change led locomotion by more than 200 ms and outlasted it by about as much
span.quote: By monitoring the onset and duration of locomotor bouts, we found that changes in membrane potential dynamics of auditory cortical excitatory neurons preceded locomotion on average by >200 ms and typically outlasted locomotion by a similar duration

span.label: tone-evoked synaptic responses were suppressed during movement, opposite to the visual cortex
span.quote: In contrast to findings in the visual cortex, stimulus (i.e., tone)-evoked synaptic responses of auditory cortical excitatory neurons were significantly diminished during movements

span.label: PV and other fast-spiking cells increased firing before movement while excitatory cells decreased
span.quote: Before and during movements, the firing rates of PV+ cells and other fast-spiking interneurons increased, whereas the firing rates of putative excitatory neurons decreased

span.label: the firing order was M2 at -870 ms, PV at -805 ms, other inhibitory at -605 ms and excitatory at -490 ms
span.quote: As a population, inhibitory neuron firing rates increased well before movement onset and also before the firing rates of auditory cortical excitatory cells decreased below their baseline levels (−805 ms for PV+ cells, −605 ms for VGAT+ cells, and −490 ms for excitatory cells, relative to movement onset).

span.label: M2 cells defined by their projection to auditory cortex behaved like the general M2 population
span.quote: Two-photon calcium imaging of GCaMP6s-expressing M2 neurons in head-fixed mice running on a treadmill revealed that M2 ACtx cells exhibited movement-related increases in fluorescence with a time course indistinguishable from that of the general M2 population

span.label: activating M2 terminals in resting mice reproduced the movement-like dynamics
span.quote: Following viral infection of AAV-ChR2 in M2 ( Extended Data Fig. 8d ), optically activating ChR2+ M2 terminals in the auditory cortex of resting mice decreased the membrane potential variability and tone-evoked responses of excitatory cells and also resulted in a slight depolarization, highly similar to the effects of movement

span.label: silencing ipsilateral M2 restored rest-like dynamics within about 70 ms, while contralateral silencing did nothing until movement stopped
span.quote: Notably, silencing ipsilateral M2 rapidly (~70 ms after laser onset) restored rest-like membrane potential dynamics in the auditory cortex ( Fig. 5f–h ), and this reversion to a rest-like state always preceded movement offset ( Fig. 5f , Extended Data Fig. 8f ). In contrast, silencing contralateral M2 did not lead to changes in auditory cortical excitatory neurons until after movement offset, effectively recapitulating the time course observed after spontaneous movement cessation

span.label: APPORTIONED, NOT EXCLUDED: about 60 percent of the suppression arises inside auditory cortex, measured from the slope relating optogenetic to tone suppression
span.quote: We also found that the degree of suppression of optogenetically evoked activity during movement was linearly related to the degree of suppression of tone-evoked activity during movement (slope = 0.6), indicating that approximately 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses in auditory cortical excitatory neurons arises through mechanisms local to the auditory cortex

span.label: ASSAY VALIDATED BEFORE THE NULL: high-frequency stimulation was shown to reduce EPSP onset slope before the absence of such a change during movement was claimed
span.quote: To explore this possibility we first established that optogenetically stimulating auditory thalamocortical synapses at > 20 Hz was sufficient to decrease the onset slope of the evoked EPSP, which provides a postsynaptic readout of presynaptic depression

span.label: CONTROL NULL: EPSP onset slope did not differ between movement and rest, so thalamic terminals are not depressed during movement
span.quote: We then measured the onset slope of optogenetically-evoked thalamocortical synaptic potentials, and found no difference in the rising slope of the EPSP across movement and rest conditions, indicating that thalamic terminals in the auditory cortex are not depressed during movement

span.label: CONFOUND EXCLUDED TWO WAYS: the terminal-activation effect survived TTX silencing of M2 somata and was faster than antidromic propagation
span.quote: Second, the onset of changes in auditory cortical dynamics following optogenetic activation of M2 terminals occurred more rapidly (<7 ms) than the antidromic propagation time from auditory cortex to M2 (~12 ms)

span.label: DECOUPLING EXPERIMENT: with ipsilateral M2 silenced the cortex returned to a rest-like state while the mouse was still moving, and tones then recovered about 40 percent of their response

span.quote: Together, these experiments dissociate the motor-related modulations we observe in the auditory cortex from movement, and show that activity in ipsilateral M2 plays a critical role in driving movement-like synaptic dynamics and controlling the gain of sensory-evoked responses in the auditory cortex.
